title: Thermodynamic description of worldwide distribution of energy and carbon emission
authors: Klaus M. Frahm, Dima L. Shepelyansky
abstract: Based on public data, we analyze the distributions of energy and carbon emission over world countries on a scale of the last 40-50 years using their presentation via Lorenz and Pareto curves. These curves in rescaled format remain remarkably stable on this time period being characterized by high values of the Gini coefficient indicating a strong inequality of energy distribution. To explain these distributions, we introduce the ENergy Thermalization Hypothesis (ENTH) according to which these distributions result from the Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) thermalization and condensation of agents representing different countries. We show that this hypothesis provides an excellent description of Lorenz and Pareto curves obtained from data on the above time period. It also gives natural grounds for inequality relating it to the RJ condensation at low energy states. We additionally trace parallels with the wealth inequality in the world.
summary: This paper applies advanced concepts from statistical mechanics, specifically Rayleigh-Jeans thermalization, to model the global distribution of energy and carbon emissions. It finds that these distributions exhibit persistent, high levels of inequality, which are accurately described by a universal thermodynamic hypothesis. This suggests that macro-scale resource allocation follows fundamental physical laws governing energy condensation.
main_problem: The paper analyzes the worldwide distribution of energy and carbon emission across countries over decades to determine the underlying physical principles governing global inequality.
main_result: The Energy Thermalization Hypothesis (ENTH), based on Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) thermalization, provides an excellent description for the observed Lorenz and Pareto curves for energy and carbon emissions. This suggests that global resource distribution follows universal thermodynamic laws characterized by strong inequality.
method: The authors use statistical mechanics concepts, specifically applying RJ thermal distributions to model socio-economic data like energy consumption and $	ext{CO}_2$ emissions.
model_or_system: The system models world countries as interacting agents whose energy/carbon distribution is governed by principles analogous to thermalization (RJ condensation). The analysis compares theoretical predictions derived from the RJE model against real World Input-Output Database (WID) data.
key_observables: Lorenz curves, Pareto distributions, Gini coefficient ($G$), and relative differences ($\Delta$) between modeled and observed energy/carbon emissions.
important_parameters: The Gini coefficients are consistently high ($G \approx 0.87-0.90$), indicating strong inequality; the RJE model parameters include $a$ and $\varepsilon$.
main_assumptions: It is assumed that only collective interactions at the country level affect global energy distribution, and the analysis relies on public datasets for energy/carbon emissions.
figures_summary: Figures show Lorenz and Pareto curves for energy/$	ext{CO}_2$ over 40-50 years demonstrating stable Gini coefficients. World maps compare model predictions ($w(	ext{RJE})_m$) to real data, highlighting relative differences ($\Delta$).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem by analyzing historical energy/carbon distributions using Lorenz/Pareto curves. It then proposes and tests the ENTH based on RJ thermalization, showing agreement with empirical data for multiple resources over decades.
why_interesting: While applied to macro-economics, the core methodology—mapping complex societal inequalities onto established physical concepts like thermalization and condensation—is a powerful analogy that touches upon non-equilibrium statistical mechanics principles relevant to open quantum systems or energy dissipation models.

The x-axis corresponds to the cumulated fraction of households/countries (h) and the y-axis to the cumulated fraction of wealth/energy consumption (w). The dashed black line corresponds to the line of perfect equipartition w = h. The Gini coefficients for the years 1984 to 2024 are G = 0.894, 0.876, 0.872, 0.875, 0.879. Right: Pareto curves C(wm) for the same data where C(wm) represents the fraction of countries with an energy consumption larger than wm (analogous to wealth). Figure 2: Lorenz curves (left panels) and Pareto curves (right panels) for the country energy consumption of the years 1994 (top) and 2024 (bottom) in the same style as in Fig. 1. Red data points correspond to the WID data [4–6] for 204 (209) countries for 1994 (2024) and blue curves correspond to the theoretical RJE curves obtained by matching Gini coefficients to determine ε and an optimal Lorenz curve fit to determine the parameter a. The parameters for 1994 are G = 0.875, ε = ⟨wm⟩RJE = 0.0166, a = 3.44 and ⟨wm⟩1994−data = 484 TWh. The parameters for 2024 are G = 0.879, ε = ⟨wm⟩RJE = 0.0105, a = 4.23 and ⟨wm⟩2024−data = 841 TWh.

Figure 3: Left: World map of effective RJE energy consumption values w(RJE) m for 209 countries computed from the blue RJE Lorenz curve (in left bottom panel) of Fig. 2 at a = 4.23, ε = 0.0105 corresponding to the best RJE fit of real 2024 WID energy consumption data [6] (see text and Fig. 13 of [11] for details). The color values shown in the color bar correspond to the ratio w(RJE) m /w(RJE) max where the maximal value corresponds to China.
